t: Research Bite #61: A Scoping Review of 20 Years of Research on Differentiation
q: This scoping review examines twenty years of academic research on the educational practice of differentiation, a method used to address student diversity in mainstream classrooms.
The authors analysed 34 peer-reviewed studies published between 1999 and 2019 to understand how this pedagogical approach is defined, implemented, and measured.
Their findings reveal significant terminological confusion, noting that the term is frequently applied to incompatible practices like ability streaming or segregation.

t: Benchmarking the Pedagogical Knowledge of Large Language Models Maria Jose Ogando Portela, Jared Lee, Paul Atherton, Robin A. A. Ince, and Oliver G. B. Garrod

q: After reviewing the LLM benchmark literature we did not find any existing LLM benchmarks which explicitly focus on knowledge of pedagogy, such as understanding of learning theories, instructional design and teaching practices.

This is a set of 920 multiple choice questions (MCQs) from teacher training exams, which evaluate LLM’s cross-domain pedagogical knowledge (CDPK). We also provide a benchmark focusing on Special Educational Needs and Disability (SEND), which consists of a further 223 questions focussed on this area.

Accuracies range from 28% (Llama-3.2 1B) to 89% for the current leader, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro model. Closed-source models dominate at the top of the leaderboard (Figure 6), with 9 out of the top 10 being closed models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic.
Based on the results of more than 25,000 teachers from 2017 to 2021, the mean expected score of a human trainee teacher would be expected to be approximately 50% on The Pedagogy Benchmark.

Previous benchmarks focus on content knowledge, measuring what models know about subject matter. Evaluating pedagogical knowledge reveals what models understand about how that content can be effectively taught and assessed.

These benchmarks do not, and cannot, measure the many other critical practical dimensions of teaching, such as classroom management, student-teacher relationships, and the ability to inspire and motivate learners, all of which are fundamental to effective teaching practice.

The increasing capability of these models brings risks of misuse, such as promoting over-reliance among novice teachers, creating an illusion of expertise that could lead to harm if incorrect advice is followed, or propagating the subtle cultural and pedagogical biases inherent in their training data.

t: Research Bite #60: Teacher-Student Relationships and Student Outcomes

t: The Good and Bad of Replaying Conversations in Your Head
q: Rerunning the tape” lets leaders analyze what transpired and consider alternative responses and statements that might be better next time.
In most cases, replaying a conversation is a healthy way to emotionally process a social exchange, revealing more accurately how the interaction made the leader feel and why.
Replaying entire conversations over and over reinforces negative thinking. No new conclusions are drawn, but the repetition quickly amplifies any negative thoughts and self-criticism.
This type of “post-event processing” strengthens the brain’s association between social situations and threat, making future interactions seem riskier.
When the replay becomes chronic, it can fuel lower self-esteem, higher anxiety, and depression. It can even interfere with sleep as thoughts of the conversation interrupt slumber.
The line between healthy and unhealthy is thin. Whether the replay is problem-solving or problem-creating is up to the person doing the thinking.

t: Looking at Working Memory Another Way
q: Working Memory can be described simply as a limited-capacity mental space where we actively and temporarily manipulate information. Its most recognised features are the limited capacity and the resulting experience of cognitive load. Yet neither is the core feature.
Functional capacity is limited to an average of about seven familiar symbols, such as digits, letters, or words, but only two to four unfamiliar ones. Distractions reduce processing capacity.
In this model, working memory is not a separate store but a function that arises from interactions between incoming stimuli and activated portions of long-term memory within the focus of attention.

New ideas always build on existing ones. A new block "lands" on an existing knowledge base. Creating a pyramid shape represents 'meaning making' - each block can "land" in different places, but when it stacks correctly on relevant prior knowledge and forms a new pyramid, it makes sense!

Because there is little to no relevant prior knowledge, the activated portions of LTM are randomly scattered and unconnected to the new items. The chances for meaningful binding are therefore low, and the activity is unlikely to leave a trace after attention fades.

In this situation, the four words are part of a well-developed expert network. Each word activates not only a single chunk, represented by a larger cemented triangle, but also a broader network of related concepts.

Viewed this way, working memory justifies its name: it's memory at work. It's a function, not a store. The key mechanism is the simultaneous activation of incoming stimuli and existing knowledge structures, which together shape the potential for later memory and performance.

t: How To Handle A High Energy Class

It also signals to students that you know what you’re doing. They can relax because a competent leader is running the classroom.

t: Empowerment Isnt All-or-Nothing
q: When highly autocratic organizations attempt to shift to a more inclusive and empowering culture, leaders often get stuck on the idea that empowerment is all-or-nothing.
Empowerment operates along a continuum. Leaders must choose where along this continuum they want to empower others.

Total Empowerment is usually reserved for experienced team members with a track record for excellence. It requires deep trust and confidence, usually earned over the course of many successful projects.
By articulating what defines success but still leaving it up to the team member regarding how to achieve the outcomes, leaders empower, but less so than handing a project off without any direction.
On the far right of the continuum is Total Direction. This is where the leader maintains complete control of the project and directs all its working parts, from goals to tactics.
Empowering others occurs along a continuum of control. The best leaders cede the most control they can as often as they can.

t: The Secret to Crystal-Clear Explanations: The NPPPN Sequence
q: When you present a wall of examples, you invite cognitive overload. Instead, present a sequence, one item at a time, to help students build a robust mental model.
There should be minimal variation when changing from a negative (N) to a positive (P) example, or vice versa, this draws students’ attention to the single thing that has changed.
Max variation between Positive examples: Show the breadth of the concept.
Min variation between Negative and Positive examples: Show the fine line between what is the concept and what is not.
This technique finds its roots in the seminal 1982 book The Theory of Instruction by Siegfried Engelmann and Douglas Carnine.

t: Teaching Backwards From the Mind
q: Tutoring had none of that. A student would arrive with a question they couldn't do, and the entire session would grow outward from that question. I wasn't delivering content. The tutor just asks. 'OK, what's an indirect tax?' The student answers correctly — fine, move on. The tutor probes further. Well, who actually pays VAT: the shopper or the business?' The student says the shopper. The tutor asks whether a business might absorb some of the increase rather than pass it all on. The student hasn't considered that. Leaders who practice stillness develop discernment that guides their entire leadership approach.” Archived from Substack on May 2, 2026 by Tim.

t: How to Articulate Your Contributions as a Senior Leader
q: The hardest leadership contributions to articulate are the ones that are most important.
Your impact as a senior leader is largely in the decisions you influence others to make.
Growth you create in others is an invisible but profound contribution to the organization.
Communicating your impact requires stepping back and seeing influence, not just activity.
The most important senior leader contributions are often the hardest to make visible.
Learning to name your influence is critical for senior leader effectiveness and advancement.
Senior leaders often underestimate the impact of their influence on organizational decisions.
The contribution that matters most is often the one you're not getting credit for.
Impact at the senior level is measured by what others accomplish because of your guidance.
Articulating senior leader impact requires shifting from activity to influence.” Archived from Unknown on May 2, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Zero-Sum Rule of High-Performing Teams
q: The Zero-Sum Rule is a structure that allows teams to focus on the most important issues and priorities by resisting the subtle creep of new things. Any new initiatives, goals, or priorities must replace existing ones.

Rather than treating time, talent, assets, and attention as unlimited resources, the rule acknowledges that team capacity is finite. By making addition require subtraction, leaders prevent quiet overload and strategic drift.
When the team must remove something to add something, everything takes on a sharper focus. By concentrating resources and energy, teams make better progress.
Team members often experience hidden stress from competing priorities and constant urgency. When leaders eliminate lower-value work, it signals respect for everyone's time and cognitive load.
Teams often add best when they subtract first.” Archived from Admired Leadership Substack on May 3, 2026 by Tim.

t: A Simple, End-of-Week Reflective Writing Activity for Secondary Students
q: It gets students reflecting on how the week went, which is right in line with Strategy #8 in The Will to Learn, Unpack Outcomes, Good or Bad.

such reflection is excellent practice for the development of the Effort and Efficacy beliefs, as students have to point their mind towards: A) What they did in the past week (i.e., their specific efforts and lack of efforts). B) What kind of results that produced.
Secondary students don't get nearly as much time for this in school as they need.
It allows students to think and write about both their academic (prompts 1-3) and non-academic (prompt 4) lives, which is great for Belonging.
It provides the teacher with lots of insight into how students are doing in terms of goal clarity, application of effort, motivation, need for assistance, and even at home.

since it's provisional writing (bottom of the Pyramid of Writing), I'd not be closely reading these or grading them but rather looking for anything concerning or noteworthy. The information I'd glean would be great soil for next week's moments of genuine connection (MGCs), Woodenization attempts, and so on.

t: Research Bite #57: Attention Hijacked: How Social Media Notifications Disrupt Cognitive Processing
q: This study investigates how social media notifications act as digital hijackers that disrupt cognitive processing and task performance.
In an ecologically valid experiment, researchers found that alerts cause a temporary slowdown in reaction time, lasting roughly 7 seconds.
This interference is driven by a combination of perceptual salience, learned conditioning, and the personal relevance of the notification.
The severity of this disruption is most accurately predicted by a user's frequency of interaction—specifically, notification volume and checking habits—rather than total screen time.

These behavioural findings were supported by physiological data, as pupil dilation patterns confirmed that more relevant notifications trigger higher levels of arousal. Ultimately, the research suggests that habitual smartphone use sensitises the brain to these digital cues, making them difficult to ignore even when they lack immediate importance.

t: Letting Your Language Take the Temperature Up and Down in a Room
q: Groups are emotional systems. When anxiety, anger, or excitement spikes too high, decision-making suffers. When emotional energy is too low, team members disengage or allow distractions to creep in.
Because a leader’s emotions are largely contagious, learning how to adjust and regulate their own behavior is the key.
It is their language, even more than their content and nonverbal posturing, that subtly raises or quickly reduces emotion.

Leaders who purposely use more intense, vivid, and emotionally laden language raise the temperature in the room. When they become animated in their use of this intense language, the energy in the room rises quickly.
For example, a leader who is seldom profane can light a fire when they choose to use such language, although for many leaders, this is not a tactic they are comfortable with.
Sometimes, good leaders move the room without lifting a finger.

t: Gradually and Then Suddenly
q: Leaders generally don’t lose the confidence of their team, reach burnout, or create a toxic culture — among many other outcomes — all at once. These happen slowly over time through dozens or hundreds of small choices, actions, and compromises.
The leadership lesson in “gradually and then suddenly” is essentially about attention.

Because the status, power, and influence wielded by leaders inhibit team members from giving them the unvarnished truth, they often march along believing in a reality that doesn’t match what is really going on.
This false or incomplete sense of reality corrupts how leaders think about the problems and challenges the organization faces, or even what problems exist.
Unfiltered information lives at the edges of the organization—with frontline team members, customers, external experts, and people who have chosen to exit the organization.
